name: content
purpose: The canonical model for every piece of learning material, whatever skill it belongs to: content items, immutable versions, media links, taxonomy, CEFR levelling, and the authoring workflow that takes a draft to publication.
context: This module exists so that vocabulary, grammar, reading, listening, speaking and writing do **not** each reinvent items, versions, media and tagging. Getting it right in Phase 2 makes Phase 3 six thin modules; getting it wrong makes Phase 3 six copies of Phase 2 (ADR-0015).
businessPurpose: Content is the product. Producing it is the real bottleneck, not writing code — so the authoring workflow, review gate and publishing pipeline are first-class features, not admin afterthoughts.
responsibilities: `content_items` — the identity of a piece of material, independent of its revisions
`content_versions` — immutable snapshots; a published lesson references a version, never a mutable item
The authoring state machine: draft → in_review → approved → published → archived
Taxonomy: topic, skill, CEFR level, exam relevance, tags
Media asset references and TTS pre-generation on publish
Content-level cache invalidation and search reindexing on publish
Level estimation assistance (AI-suggested, human-approved)
notResponsibilities: Skill-specific item shape and grading — that belongs to each skill module
Sequencing content into a course — that is `lesson`
Deciding what a learner sees next — that is `learning`

rules: A published version is immutable. Editing published material creates a new version; the old one stays live until the new one is published.
A learner never sees a draft. Every learner-facing query filters `status = 'published'`.
An author cannot approve their own version — review requires a different admin.
Publishing is blocked until every referenced media asset is processed and verified.
Archiving is blocked while a published lesson still references the version (`CONTENT_IN_USE`).
CEFR level is required before review; an AI suggestion is a starting point, never the final value.
`body` is validated against a JSON schema chosen by `kind`, so a skill module's payload cannot be malformed.
Publishing invalidates the content cache, enqueues TTS generation, and triggers reindexing — all through the outbox so a failure in one does not roll back the publish.
Slugs are immutable after first publication; a changed slug would break external links and bookmarks.

stateMachine.description: The authoring workflow. The transition that matters most is `Published → Draft`: creating a new version does **not** take the live version down.
stateMachine.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft: create
    Draft --> InReview: submit
    InReview --> Draft: changes requested
    InReview --> Approved: approved by a different admin
    Approved --> Draft: withdrawn
    Approved --> Published: publish
    Published --> Draft: new version started (live version stays up)
    Published --> Archived: archive (blocked if in use)
    Archived --> Draft: clone into a new version

    note right of Published
        On publish, via the outbox:
        · invalidate content cache
        · enqueue TTS generation
        · reindex for search
        · emit content.published
    end note

flows.title: Publish
flows.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor AD as Admin
    participant C as content
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant OB as outbox
    participant ME as media
    participant SE as search
    participant CA as cache

    AD->>C: POST /admin/content/{id}/publish
    C->>C: require content.publish; state must be Approved
    C->>ME: are all referenced assets processed?
    alt not ready
        C-->>AD: 409 MEDIA_NOT_READY
    else ready
        C->>DB: BEGIN
        C->>DB: version.status = published; item.current_version_id = version
        C->>DB: INSERT outbox(content.published)
        C->>DB: COMMIT
        C-->>AD: 200
        OB->>CA: invalidate content keys
        OB->>ME: enqueue TTS for new text
        OB->>SE: reindex
    end

decisions.question: Shared content model or per-skill models?
decisions.why: Six near-identical models would diverge within a year and make mixed-skill lessons impossible. The genuinely different part — the grader — stays in the skill module (ADR-0015)

decisions.question: Mutable content or versions?
decisions.why: A learner's attempt must be interpretable against the material they actually saw; editing published material in place would silently rewrite history

decisions.question: Who assigns the CEFR level?
decisions.why: Levelling is a pedagogical judgement with real consequences for learner experience; the model proposes, the author disposes

decisions.question: Who may read published content, and who may change it?
decisions.choice: Any signed-in learner reads; only an administrator writes
decisions.why: Published material is the first thing a learner reads that is not their own data, so `self` cannot express it and it needs a named permission — `content.read.published`, held by the `user` role. Leaving the reads anonymous would hand a whole course to anyone with the URL and remove the surface Phase 4 attaches entitlements to. Create, edit, review, publish and archive stay with `admin` (migration 1700000180)

decisions.question: Where does `archived` live — on the item or on the version?
decisions.why: A version is an immutable snapshot, and `trg_content_versions_immutable` refuses every UPDATE once it is published — including a status change — so `content_versions.status` can never become `archived`. Archiving sets `content_items.status`. The consequence the reads must honour: a published version stays `published` forever, so filtering only on the version status returns archived material; every learner-facing query joins `content_items` and filters there as well (P7.2)

decisions.question: What happens to a learner mid-session when the item is archived?
decisions.choice: Version stays readable by direct ID, hidden from discovery only
decisions.why: A learner who opened a lesson holds a version ID. Archiving must not 404 that learner's session; GetVersion by ID has no status filter and remains readable (P7.3 integration test step 12). Discovery queries (Browse, GetPublishedVersionBySlug, Count) join content_items and filter status='published', so archived material disappears from lists. Recorded in P7.3 per its trap.

decisions.question: Bind activities to items or versions?
decisions.why: A learner's attempt must be interpretable against exactly what they saw; item binding would let a republish change the meaning of past results

decisions.question: Where do unlocking rules live?
decisions.why: The rule is structural (a property of the curriculum); the state is personal (a property of the learner). Splitting them keeps both modules honest

decisions.question: Are the course and lesson reads public?
decisions.why: A lesson response carries its activities and their resolved content versions, so an anonymous `/lessons/{id}` publishes the whole course and removes the surface Phase 4 attaches entitlements to. The `user` role holds the read permission; writing courses and reordering activities stays with `admin`

decisions.question: How to invalidate the catalogue cache without wildcards?
decisions.why: The catalogue key has one hash per level/limit/offset permutation. Storing a generation counter in Redis and bumping it on publish invalidates all filter combinations instantly without an expensive SCAN in the request path (P7.5 Trap 1)

decisions.question: When does cache invalidation take place relative to publish?
decisions.choice: Synchronously in service post-commit, plus outbox event backstop
decisions.why: Outbox events reach subscribers through `cmd/worker`, so an event-only invalidation leaves a window in which an author reloads the course and still sees the pre-publish tree. `PublishLesson` therefore deletes the keys itself once the transaction commits; Redis is shared, so that delete is visible to every process immediately. A `lesson.published` consumer in the worker repeats it as the backstop for a delete that failed while Redis was unreachable — a failed delete only warns, it never fails the publish (P7.5 Traps 2 and 3)

rules: Scoring happens on the server. The client never sends a score, only a response.
An attempt is immutable once graded. A retake creates a new attempt; the history is kept.
A grader is selected by activity kind from a registry populated at startup; an unknown kind is a startup error.
Asynchronous graders (writing, speaking) return `Async: true`; the attempt stays `grading` until the completing event arrives.
Submitting requires an `Idempotency-Key`; a replay returns the original result rather than creating a second attempt.
Progress rolls up on completion: activity → lesson → unit → course, in one transaction.
A lesson is complete when every required activity is complete; optional activities do not block it.
Attempts older than the activity's time limit are expired by a job and cannot be submitted.
Skill mastery is an exponentially weighted estimate over recent attempts, not a raw average — recent performance must dominate.
The placement test adapts: item difficulty follows the running estimate, and it stops when the confidence interval is narrow enough or the item budget is exhausted.

decisions.question: One engine or per-skill flows?
decisions.why: Attempt lifecycle, idempotency, progress rollup and event emission are identical across skills; only scoring differs. Six copies would drift and each would need its own idempotency bug fixed separately

decisions.question: Where do review items come from?
decisions.why: Only the grader knows what was actually tested; `srs` should not have to reverse-engineer that from a score

decisions.question: Server-side scoring only?
decisions.why: Client-side scoring is trivially manipulable, and progress data that cannot be trusted is worthless for both the learner and analytics

decisions.question: Where does the idempotency key travel on attempt submission?
decisions.choice: Required `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header with UUIDv7 format
decisions.why: ADR-0015 requires idempotent submission. Carrying it in the standard HTTP header makes it part of the formal OpenAPI contract rather than an internal backend detail, enabling clients to safely retry on network failure (P8.1 Trap 2)

decisions.question: Single-lesson or batched lock checking in `UnlockChecker`?
decisions.why: Rendering a course detail fetches lock status for all lessons in the course (e.g. 40 lessons). Batching avoids an N+1 call into learning and matches the pattern established by `content.Reader.GetManyVersions` (P8.1 Trap 3)

decisions.question: What is the asynchronous attempt state called?
decisions.why: WP8 P8.3 calls it `pending` in prose. The wire name is `grading`, because the client shows "being marked" and `pending` is what an unsubmitted attempt would sound like. Recorded because a name that differs between the work package and the spec is found the day the handler is written (P8.1)

decisions.question: Which module owns `ReviewItem` returned by `ExerciseGrader`?
decisions.why: All six skill modules implement `ExerciseGrader` and return `GradeResult`. If `ReviewItem` came from `srs`, modules like reading/listening/speaking/writing would violate architecture boundary rules by depending on `c_srs`. Boundary mapping to `srs` occurs in `learning` service (P8.1 Trap 1)

decisions.question: How is submission idempotency enforced on partitioned `attempts`?
decisions.choice: A conditional claim on the attempt row, not a unique index on the key
decisions.why: A unique constraint on a partitioned table must include the partition key, so `UNIQUE (idempotency_key)` is unavailable and `UNIQUE (idempotency_key, created_at)` would hold only within one calendar month. The invariant that matters is narrower: **one attempt row is graded at most once**. `ClaimAttemptForGrading` carries `AND status = 'in_progress'`, so of two concurrent submissions exactly one updates the row and the other returns no rows — the database arbitrates, not a check-then-write in the service. The loser reads the attempt back: a matching `idempotency_key` means its own retry already succeeded and the stored result is the answer, a different one is a conflict. Proved by `TestLearningSchema_OneAttemptIsGradedAtMostOnce`, which fails with 2 of 2 claims when the status guard is removed (P8.2 Trap 1)

decisions.question: What mechanism and lock ID schedules monthly partition rotation?
decisions.why: Repository schedules periodic maintenance through `internal/platform/job` with advisory locks, not River. Lock ID `1_700_000_210` matches migration `1700000210` and is unique across all modules. Rotation runs periodically and at worker boot to prevent partition lapse outages (P8.2 Traps 3 and 4)

decisions.question: How is an activity resolved across course hierarchy without cross-module SQL joins?
decisions.why: Resolving an activity ID to its kind, content_version_id, lesson_id, unit_id, course_id and skill_focus in one call avoids three round trips per attempt on the hottest path in the product, preserving DB1/DB2 module boundaries without cross-schema joins (P8.3 Trap 1)

decisions.question: How is the grader registry validated at startup — against the kinds in the database, or the kinds the module declares?
decisions.choice: Registry-declared: `Deps.DeclaredKinds` checked against the registered graders in `New`
decisions.why: ADR-0015 requires the registry validated at startup and P8.3 §4 offers two readings. Registry-complete would have `cmd/api` read `learn.activities.kind` at boot, which makes a content author able to stop the next deploy — `kind` is free text bounded only by length. Registry-declared splits the two failures by who caused them: a wiring mistake, where a deployment claims a kind it registered no grader for, stops the process in `New` with the kind named; data asking for a kind nobody declared fails that one request with `UNSUPPORTED_ACTIVITY_KIND` (422), also naming the kind. What neither reading permits is a registry returning nil for an unknown kind, so `Get` reports absence and the service never dispatches to nil. Phase 2 declares nothing because WP9 writes the first real grader, and `New` registers nothing it was not handed (P8.3 Trap 2)

decisions.question: Is `m_learning` one arch-lint component or four?
decisions.choice: Four, against P8.3 §2's instruction to inherit the single one
decisions.why: The brief says `m_learning` is one component and "you inherit that". It stops being possible the moment the module has more than one package: with `in: modules/learning/**`, go-arch-lint treats every package under it as its own import target, so module.go importing `learning/service` is a component-to-component dependency and is rejected. Naming the component in its own `mayDependOn` does not help — both forms were tried and both produce the same ten violations. Every module in this repository that has real layered code (`auth`, `rbac`, `audit`, `admin`, `content`, `lesson`) is split the same way; the `**` form survives only while a module is a single package, which is what `learning` was when the brief was written. The package layout still follows `lesson`'s, which is what §9 actually asks for (P8.3 §2)

decisions.question: Why does `GradeRequest` carry only IDs?
decisions.choice: Pass IDs only, let graders read what they need
decisions.why: Carrying resolved content in GradeRequest couples all six skill modules to content representations and makes interface evolution impossible; passing IDs preserves clean boundaries (P8.3 Trap 3)

decisions.question: How does asynchronous grading behave on submit?
decisions.choice: Returns 202 Accepted with status `grading`, leaving score unset
decisions.why: Synchronous graders answer 200 with score; AI-based graders (writing, speaking) return Async: true, which preserves grading status until completed by asynchronous event consumers in Phase 3 (P8.3 Trap 5)

decisions.question: What does a duplicate submission see while the caller holding the claim is still grading?
decisions.choice: It waits, bounded, for that transaction to commit and then returns the stored result
decisions.why: The grade, the rollup and the status change are one transaction, so until it commits the duplicate reads the row as `ClaimAttemptForGrading` left it — `grading`, with no score. Answering from that read returned `async: true` and a 202 for an activity whose grader is synchronous, so the two callers of one submission got different bodies; CI caught it as a failing assertion, not a race. `awaitSettledAttempt` re-reads for up to 40 × 5 ms. The bound is not an error path: a grader that really is asynchronous never settles, and 202 is the right answer then. Proved by `TestSubmitAttempt_DuplicateWaitsForTheClaimHolder`, which forces the window with a grader that parks and a hook on the repository's reads, and fails on the `async` assertion with the wait removed (P8.3 Trap 4)

decisions.question: What does a replayed submission return for `feedback`?
decisions.choice: Null — the stored attempt has no prose to read back
decisions.why: P8.3 Trap 4 asks the loser of the claim to return the stored result rather than a fresh grade. `learn.attempts` stores `score`, `max_score`, `grader`, `duration_ms` and `status`, and P8.2 created no column for the grader's prose, so score and status replay exactly and `feedback` cannot. It briefly returned the constant `domain.FakeGrader` happens to emit, which matched the winner's body only while the fake was the only grader and told a learner who scored 0 that they were correct. Null is the honest answer; making the bodies identical needs a `feedback` column, which is a schema change this task does not own (P8.3 Trap 4)

decisions.question: How is progress rollup and event emission coordinated?
decisions.choice: Single database transaction enclosing attempt update, progress rollup, and outbox event writes
decisions.why: Atomic progress update across activity, lesson, unit, and course boundaries ensures partial rollups cannot occur; outbox writes inside the transaction guarantee event delivery without dual-write race conditions (P8.3 Trap 6)

decisions.question: How are lesson prerequisites checked for unlocking?
decisions.choice: Batched: `lesson.Reader.ListPrerequisitesForLessons` for the rules, `learning`’s own progress for the answer, with `min_score` enforced
decisions.why: `learn.lesson_prerequisites` belongs to `lesson` and `learn.progress` belongs to `learning`, so neither module can answer alone and a SQL join across the two would break DB1 silently. `lesson` keeps its locally declared consumer interface — `m_lesson_service` still may not depend on `c_learning` — and only its signature changed to the batched shape. Unlocked means the prerequisite is complete **and** scored at or above `min_score`: a checker that reads only the status unlocks a lesson for a learner who failed the one before it (P8.4 Trap 1)

decisions.question: Which enrolment statuses may be written?
decisions.why: The OpenAPI enum admits `active`, `completed` and `paused`, while the CHECK constraint admits `active`, `completed` and `dropped`, so `paused` cannot be stored and `dropped` cannot be returned, and nothing in CI compares the two. The intersection is the two values Phase 2 actually needs; nothing here pauses or drops an enrolment. `uq_enrollments_user_course` makes a second enrolment a 409 `ALREADY_ENROLLED`, mapped from the constraint rather than raced in the service, and a course id with no course is a 404 `COURSE_NOT_FOUND` mapped from `fk_enrollments_course` (P8.4 Trap 2)

decisions.question: When is a course complete?
decisions.choice: When every unit in it is complete — not when its last lesson is
decisions.why: `rollupCourse` asked `NextLesson(course, currentLesson) == nil`, which is “is this the last lesson”, not “is the course finished”: a learner who opened only the final unit and completed it published `course.completed` with two thirds of the course untouched, and `gamification` and `analytics` consume that event in Phase 3. The rollup now reads unit-scope progress for every unit of the course, and flips `enrollments.status` to `completed` with `completed_at` in the same transaction as the course progress row and the outbox write (P8.4 Trap 3)

decisions.question: How is mastery estimated across attempts?
decisions.choice: Exponentially weighted (alpha = 0.35) onto CEFR bands, with an unrecognised skill focus skipped rather than failing the submission
decisions.why: BR-LEARNING-09 requires recent performance to dominate, so a running average is not enough. The write happens inside the grading transaction, which is why the skill is normalised first: `learn.skill_mastery.skill` is a CHECK over six values while `learn.lessons.skill_focus` is free text, and an author who types `vocab` would otherwise abort the rollup and fail the learner’s submission (P8.4 Trap 4)

decisions.question: How is a mastery estimate carried between attempts when only the band is stored?
decisions.choice: The prior estimate is read back from the band’s midpoint
decisions.why: `learn.skill_mastery` keeps `level` and `confidence` and nothing else — P8.2 created no column for a raw estimate and P8.4 adds none, because a new column is a schema change this task does not own. The estimate therefore restarts each update from the midpoint of the stored band, which loses precision inside a band but not direction: ten poor attempts still walk the level down and three strong ones walk it back up. If Phase 3’s skill radar needs the finer signal, it needs a column first (P8.4 Trap 4)

decisions.question: What does the dashboard get for a learner who has started nothing?
decisions.choice: An explicit state, never null and never a 404
decisions.why: `DashboardResponse.state` is one of `not_started`, `in_progress` and `completed`, and `next_activity` is absent in two of the three. No enrolment at all is `not_started`; enrolments that have all ended is `completed`. That is the common case during the alpha and the state the client renders as its empty screen (P8.4 Trap 5)

decisions.question: How many reads may resolving the next activity cost?
decisions.choice: One per unit in the course, never one per lesson
decisions.why: Walking the course with `NextLesson` costs a call for every lesson already finished, so a learner 39 lessons into a 40-lesson course pays 39 calls on the endpoint every app open hits — the same N+1 the batched `UnlockChecker` exists to remove, on the same page. Resolution lists the course’s units once, then the lessons of each unit, then reads only the chosen lesson. `NextActivity.title` is the lesson’s title, because `learn.activities` has no title column (P8.4 Trap 5)

decisions.question: Where does `total_activities` for a course come from?
decisions.why: `learn.progress` records one row per scope and nothing on an activity-scope row says which course the activity belongs to, so both halves of the fraction need `lesson`. Walking units → lessons → activities would cost a read per lesson on the endpoint whose acceptance is a query count, and reading `learn.activities` from this module's SQL would break DB1 where nothing in CI could see it. One call answers for every course a learner is enrolled in; `/me/progress` costs four repository reads and one contract read whatever the course count (P8.5 Trap 1)

decisions.question: What is the dashboard's query budget, exactly?
decisions.choice: Constant in lessons and activities; one `ListLessons` per unit, inherited from next-activity resolution
decisions.why: The endpoint is asserted against three fixtures: 3 units × 10 lessons, 3 units × 40 lessons and 20 units × 20 lessons. Repository reads and every contract read except `ListLessons` are identical across all three, and `ListLessons` is pinned at one per unit rather than left unasserted — P8.4 resolves the next activity by listing each unit's lessons, and collapsing that into the same batched call would be a deliberate edit to the test rather than a silent drift (P8.5 Trap 2)

decisions.question: Which key does `/me/progress` cache under, given the documented key named a course?
decisions.choice: `fluentra:{env}:learning:progress:{user_id}:v1` — one key per learner, not per course
decisions.why: The AGENT.md table was written before the endpoint: `GET /me/progress` returns every enrolled course in one response, so a key per course would need assembling from N cache entries to answer one request. The table now names what the code writes (P8.5 Trap 3)

decisions.question: How stale can a cached dashboard be after the learner's own submit?
decisions.choice: Invalidated after commit; bounded by the 2-minute TTL in one race
decisions.why: Submission, enrolment and session completion all delete the learner's dashboard and progress keys once their transaction has committed, and a failed delete is logged rather than returned so a Redis outage cannot fail a write. One window remains: `Cache.GetOrLoad` writes a loaded value back on a goroutine, so a read that started before a concurrent submit can land its pre-submit value after the delete, and the TTL is what clears it. That is the same write-back the catalogue counter avoids by using `Get`, and here it costs at most one stale dashboard for two minutes rather than a wrong lock verdict (P8.5 Trap 3)

decisions.question: What does `due_reviews_count` return in Phase 2?
decisions.choice: A literal zero, with no `srs` dependency of any kind
decisions.why: `internal/modules/srs/contract` holds one file and no types; WP9 P9.1 writes them. The field is `required` in `DashboardResponse`, so it is present and zero rather than omitted, and `m_learning_service` still may not depend on `c_srs` — that edge belongs to WP9's diff, with WP9's test behind it (P8.5 Trap 4)

decisions.question: How are a course's progress status and percentage derived?
decisions.choice: Integer division truncating toward zero, and a status that is not the enrolment status
decisions.why: `percentage` is `completed * 100 / total`, truncating, and `0/0` is 0 rather than a panic or a 100. `CourseProgress.status` is one of `not_started`, `in_progress` and `completed` and is derived from the activity counts plus a completed enrolment — deliberately not the enrolment's own `active` / `completed`, which answers a different question (P8.5 Traps 1 and 5)

decisions.question: How are learning sessions timed, and who may complete one?
decisions.choice: The server computes the minutes; a session belonging to another learner is a 404
decisions.why: `CompleteSessionRequest` carries only `activities_completed`, so the duration is derived from `started_at` and the clock — a client-supplied duration is the same class of mistake as a client-supplied score (BR-LEARNING-01). A negative activity count is rejected as `INVALID_ACTIVITY_COUNT` before the CHECK constraint turns it into a 500, and `learning.session_completed` is written to the outbox inside the completing transaction (P8.4 Trap 6)

rules: Scheduling is FSRS, implemented in `domain/` as pure functions with no I/O — it must be testable and provable without a database.
Grades are exactly four: `again`, `hard`, `good`, `easy`. Do not add a fifth without reading the algorithm's assumptions.
A card's next due date depends only on its state, the grade, the elapsed time and the parameters — never on the time of day or the session.
Reviews answered before they are due update stability but do not shorten the schedule punitively; early review is allowed and modelled.
Daily new-card and review limits are per learner and enforced when building the session, not by refusing an answer mid-session.
A session interleaves skills and avoids presenting two cards from the same word family consecutively.
A lapse (grading `again` on a mature card) reduces stability according to the algorithm — it does not reset to zero.
Suspended cards never appear in a queue and are excluded from forecasts.
Every answer writes a review log; the log is the raw material for future parameter optimisation and must never be pruned before the retention window.
The scheduler is versioned: a parameter change records the version on each log so past scheduling remains explainable.

limitations: Parameters are global in Phase 2; per-learner optimisation needs several hundred reviews per learner and arrives later.

conventions: All scheduling logic lives in `domain/fsrs.go` as pure functions. If a scheduling decision needs a database read, the design is wrong.

decisions.question: FSRS or SM-2?
decisions.why: Explicit stability and difficulty modelling, published parameters, and materially fewer reviews for the same retention. SM-2 is simpler but leaves measurable learning value on the table (ADR-0016)

decisions.question: Four grades or six?
decisions.why: The algorithm is defined for four; more options increase learner hesitation without improving scheduling accuracy

decisions.question: Cards reference versions or items?
decisions.why: A card must test what the learner actually learned; if the content is revised, a new card is correct

decisions.question: How does the dashboard learn the due count?
decisions.why: Keeps dashboard assembly consolidated inside learning while honoring architecture boundaries (P9.1 Decision 7.1)

decisions.choice: Post-commit via contract call with outbox backstop
decisions.why: Avoids cross-module transaction coupling; activity.completed in outbox serves as replayable backstop (P9.1 Decision 7.2)

decisions.question: Does answering a review immediately invalidate the dashboard cache?
decisions.why: Dashboard has 2-minute TTL; cross-module invalidation deferred to Phase 3 (P9.1 Decision 7.3)

decisions.why: Used by all skill graders implementing ExerciseGrader without requiring c_srs dependencies across 6 skill modules (P9.1 Decision 7.4 / Trap 1)

decisions.why: P9.1 Decision 7.5 deferred it, and the deferral produced a handler answering 200 with an empty day list — a specced endpoint telling every learner they have nothing due. The grouped query is smaller than the workaround, buckets by the learner local day like the due queue, and no screen depends on it either way

decisions.why: learn.review_cards belongs to srs. vocabulary marking a word known has to reach the due queue, and the alternative — a second suspension flag in skill.user_word_state that the due query would have to join — is the table duplication ADR-0015 exists to prevent

rules: Every explanation cites a `grammar_points.code`. An explanation the model cannot ground in a taxonomy point is discarded, not shown.

name: gamification
purpose: Motivation mechanics: XP, levels, streaks, badges, quests and leaderboards. It reacts to learning events and never drives them.
context: Gamification is downstream by design. It subscribes to events from `learning`, `srs`, `writing` and `speaking`, and owns no learning logic — so a change to how motivation works can never break how learning works.
businessPurpose: Retention in consumer learning products is decided in the first two weeks, and streaks plus visible progress are the strongest levers available. Used carelessly they produce anxiety and churn instead, so the rules below lean towards forgiveness.
responsibilities: XP awards per learning action, with anti-farming rules
Levels derived from cumulative XP
Streaks with freezes and timezone-correct day boundaries
Badges and their unlock conditions
Quests: time-boxed multi-step goals
Leaderboards (opt-in, league-based)
Daily goal tracking
notResponsibilities: Deciding what counts as learning — the source modules do

consumes.name: review.session_completed
consumes.reason: Award XP and extend the streak

rules: XP is awarded from events only, and is idempotent on (user, source, source_id) — a redelivered event must not double-award.
The streak day boundary is in the learner's own timezone, and a timezone change never retroactively breaks a streak.
A streak extends when the daily goal is met, not merely when the app is opened.
Freezes are limited and replenish slowly; a freeze is consumed automatically at the day boundary if the goal was missed and one is available.
Anti-farming: XP per source type is capped daily, and repeating the same activity yields diminishing returns.
Badges are idempotent — earning conditions are re-evaluated safely and a badge is awarded once.
Leaderboards are opt-in, display names only, and are league-based so a learner competes with peers rather than with the whole platform.
Gamification never blocks learning: running out of XP, freezes or league position must not prevent any learning action.
Streak reminders respect quiet hours and are sent by `notification`, not from here.

errors.meaning: Not an error — the award is capped and reported as such

flows.mermaid:
flowchart TD A[Nightly job, per timezone bucket] --> B{daily goal met yesterday?} B -->|yes| C[current += 1; longest = max] B -->|no| D{freeze available?} D -->|yes| E[consume a freeze; streak preserved
notify gently] D -->|no| F[streak broken → 0

tasks.title: Add a badge
steps: Add the badge with its criteria expression to the catalogue.
Implement the evaluator, which must be idempotent and cheap — it runs on many events.
Backfill for existing learners with a job if the badge is retroactive.
Add the artwork and the description copy.
Test that re-running the evaluator awards it exactly once.

limitations: Leaderboard leagues are static rather than skill-matched.
Quests are hand-authored; there is no generation from a learner's profile.
Anti-farming is rule-based and will not catch a determined script.
Streak evaluation runs per timezone bucket, so a learner who changes timezone mid-day sees an approximation.
testFocus: XP idempotency under redelivered events
Streak day boundaries across timezones and DST
Timezone change does not retroactively break a streak
Freeze consumption at the boundary
Daily caps and diminishing returns
Badge awarded exactly once under concurrent evaluation
Leaderboard excludes learners who have not opted in

decisions.question: Event-driven or called directly?
decisions.why: It keeps motivation mechanics strictly downstream — a bug here can never break a learning flow, and learning modules need no knowledge of XP at all

decisions.question: Streak freezes?
decisions.why: An all-or-nothing streak punishes the illness or travel that real learners have, and losing a long streak is a strong churn trigger. Forgiveness retains better than strictness

decisions.question: Global leaderboard?
decisions.why: A global board demotivates everyone outside the top few and creates a privacy exposure nobody asked for

decisions.question: Which day boundary does a streak use?
decisions.why: core.users already stores a timezone and the seed sets Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh. Counting in UTC would end the day at 7am local, so a learner studying in the evening in Vietnam loses a streak they kept

decisions.question: What identity appears on a league board?
decisions.choice: The display name, and only inside a league the learner opted into
decisions.why: Display name is the only name a learner chooses and the only one already meant to be seen; email and profile are never on a board. The opt-in boundary is what keeps this compatible with refusing a global leaderboard — a name is shown to people the learner joined, not to everyone

decisions.question: How much XP does a graded item award?
decisions.choice: Its best score ever, divided by ten, granted as the increase over what it has already granted
decisions.why: 80/100 grants 8. Retaking to 100/100 grants 2, not 10. A third attempt grants nothing. XP therefore measures what a learner can do rather than how many times they pressed retry, and cannot be farmed by repetition. The award is never negative: a worse retake takes nothing back

decisions.question: Where does the XP high-water mark live?
decisions.choice: In this module, not in learn.progress
decisions.why: UpsertProgress sets score = EXCLUDED.score, so learn.progress holds the most recent score and not the best one — a bad retake lowers it. XP must never fall, so it cannot be derived from that column and needs its own per-item record of what has already been granted

decisions.question: What earns XP?
decisions.choice: Lessons completed, word senses reaching known, and tests passed
decisions.why: The three things a learner does that represent knowledge rather than activity. Tests have nothing to attach to yet — the exam module is Phase 4 and its tables do not exist — so that source is declared and left unwired rather than faked
